newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Focus on NAPM prices paid.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Focus on NAPM prices paid.

text.p: U.S. credit markets on Tuesday will look to the National Association of Purchasing Management data to validate Monday's sell-off after a surprise jump in Chicago Purchasing Managers' prices paid, market experts said.

The Chicago Managers said the September price index jumped to 59.3, its highest level in more than a year, from August's 51.8. Dealers expect a similar jump in NAPM prices paid. "The Chicago prices paid has a good historical fit to NAPM prices," said Matt Alexy, chief markets strategist at CS First Boston.
Analysts stressed that prices paid is not a component of the NAPM index but rather an entirely separate piece of data.
Thus the NAPM overall index reading could be almost unchanged, as widely expected, while prices paid could jump.
A Reuter poll called for a NAPM September index reading of 52.5, little changed from August's 52.6 reading.

"If we see a (NAPM) breakdown like Chciago's with prices up and the overall (index) down just a touch, the bond market reaction will be muted," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
Analysts said the Chicago PMI and NAPM have taken on added importance as the figures seemingly give market-makers some predictive power regarding U.S. payrolls.
The highly-anticipated employment report for September is scheduled for release this Friday at 830 EDT/1230 GMT.
Dealers agreed the market overall is positioned neutral after a spate of selling on Friday shook out those holding long positions, as did Monday's mild sell-off.
"I think people are now satisfied to stay with positions they are currently holding until Friday's payrolls," Low said.
One and a half hours before the 1000 EDT/1400 GMT release of the NAPM data, August's index of leading indicators will hit the markets.
Dealers expect little market impact from the index of leading indicators, calling it a repackaging of already released August data that has been factored into trading levels.

Commodity prices, the manufacturing work week, stock prices and initial claims were the prime contributors, while broad-based declines in capital and consumer goods orders limited the gains, said NationsBanc Capital Markets.
Analysts said they will keep an eye open Tuesday afternoon for the first drop of the expected trickle of U.S. September auto sales.
A Reuter poll shows a concensus forecast for roughly 7.2 million cars and 5.7 million trucks sold in the month.
However, these figures are typically released too late in the trading day and often too piecemeal to move markets, dealers said.
